text: [Page 1]. Cross-Lingual Mechanistic Interpretability & Safety. Alignment for Low-Resource Languages (Gujarati). 1. Project Overview & Scientific Motivation. Large Language Models (LLMs) are primarily aligned and safety-tuned using English-centric. datasets. As prompts are translated into low-resource languages such as Gujarati, these safety.

mechanisms may weaken, enabling harmful requests to bypass alignment safeguards. This. phenomenon is known as the cross-lingual safety vulnerability. This project investigates the internal. safety representations of Apertus-8B, a fully open multilingual foundation model developed by the. Swiss AI Initiative (ETH Zurich, EPFL, and CSCS). The study aims to identify and analyze.

multilingual refusal vectors, evaluate whether English safety representations transfer to Gujarati,. and quantify the Jailbreak Tax, defined as the reduction in model helpfulness caused by stronger. safety alignment.. 2. Technical Architecture & Specifications. Model: Apertus-8B  Architecture: 8-billion-parameter dense Transformer optimized for multilingual. reasoning.

 Activation Function: xIELU (Expanded Integral of the Exponential Linear Unit),. designed to improve optimization stability and gradient flow in deep multilingual networks. . Compliance: Developed following Swiss transparency principles and EU AI Act requirements,. making it suitable for mechanistic interpretability and open-science research.. 3. Eight-Week Execution Timeline.

Phase 1 (Weeks 1–2): Dataset Preparation & Baseline Probing.  Construct a benchmark containing 100 prompts (50 harmful, 50 benign)..  Translate English prompts into Gujarati using an automated pipeline followed by 20% manual. verification to preserve semantic fidelity..  Validate tokenization, preprocessing, and PyTorch data-loading pipelines..

Phase 2 (Weeks 3–4): Cloud Infrastructure & Activation Extraction.  Provision an NVIDIA L40S or RTX 4090 cloud instance..  Load Apertus-8B and extract residual stream activations across all 32 Transformer layers for. English and Gujarati prompts..  Develop custom TransformerLens hooks compatible with xIELU while minimizing GPU memory. usage and preventing OOM failures..

Phase 3 (Weeks 5–6): Sparse Autoencoder & Causal Steering.  Train a lightweight Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) on layers exhibiting the highest cross-lingual. cosine similarity..  Perform activation patching experiments to test whether injecting English refusal vectors into. Gujarati forward passes causally induces safe refusal behavior.. Phase 4 (Weeks 7–8): Evaluation & Research Paper Preparation.

 Measure Gujarati jailbreak success rates, translation bypass performance, and the Jailbreak Tax..  Prepare the final manuscript in LaTeX, emphasizing reproducibility, mechanistic interpretability,. multilingual safety, and alignment with the EU AI Act and Swiss AI Initiative open-science practices..

Abstract—Object detection models routinely achieve strong. results on standard benchmarks, yet their behaviour under real-. world corruptions is much less well understood. Scalar metrics. like mean Average Precision collapse all failure information. into a single number — making it impossible to distinguish. whether a model missed detections, generated false positives, lost.

localisation precision, or became overconfident.. We introduceFailure Geometry, an evaluation framework that. represents corruption-induced degradation as a four-dimensional. failure vectorF=[∆R,∆P,∆L,∆E], capturing recall degra-. dation, precision shift, localisation error, and calibration drift.. We evaluate four pretrained detectors — YOLOv8n, YOLOv9c,.

DETR (ResNet-50), and RT-DETR — under 17 corruption types. across five severity levels ontwoindependent benchmarks: the. full COCO val2017 dataset (5,000 images) and Pascal VOC,. substantially expanding prior work which covered at most nine. corruption types on a single dataset and subsets of 500 to 2,000. images.. Our experiments surface two architecturally consistent failure.

modes that replicate across both datasets.Hallucinationunder. zoom blur — where false-positive rate increases with severity. — is confirmed on COCO for all four models (∆P=+0.264. for YOLOv9c down to+0.084for RT-DETR at severity 5). and, with attenuated magnitude, on three of four models on. VOC (YOLOv8n+0.068, DETR+0.137, YOLOv9c≈0.001),.

dataset-independent failure signatures.. Beyond replicating the taxonomy qualitatively, we introduce. three quantitative instruments that turn "does the taxonomy. transfer?" into a measurable question. from COCO to VOC (R2=0.84–0.95across three architectures),. whereas∆Pand∆Etransfer weakly and unevenly (R2as low as. 0.15for DETR), explainingwhythreshold-collapse and late-onset-. collapse — both∆R-driven — replicate reliably while hallucina-. tion does not. using single-dataset robustness rankings as deployment guidance.. Index Terms—Object detection, robustness, corruption, failure. analysis, YOLOv8, YOLOv9c, DETR, RT-DETR, calibration,. ImageNet-C, Pascal VOC, failure geometry, mCRS, cross-dataset. generalisation, transferability. I. INTRODUCTION. Deployed object detectors operate in environments that.

look nothing like the clean, well-lit, high-resolution images. on which they are evaluated. Sensors introduce noise. Video. codecs compress frames. Rain, fog, and motion blur distort. spatial structure. These corruptions are not edge cases — they. are the ordinary conditions of real deployment in autonomous. driving, industrial inspection, surveillance, and medical imag-. ing [1], [20]..

The standard response to this gap has been benchmarking:. measure how much mAP drops under each corruption type and. report the result [8]–[10]. This approach has produced valuable. empirical evidence, most notably the finding by Liuet al.that. robustness and clean accuracy are largely decoupled [10]. But. a drop in mAP tells us very little aboutwhya model failed.

or what a practitioner should do about it, and — as we show. in this work — a robustness ranking measured on a single. [Page 2]. dataset can itself be misleading if it does not transfer to a. second, independently curated benchmark.. We argue that failure analysis for object detection requires. both amulti-dimensionaland across-datasetperspective. A.

model can fail through at least four distinct mechanisms:. (i) it misses detections that were previously found (recall. degradation,∆R); (ii) it generates spurious detections that. did not previously exist (precision inflation,∆P); (iii) its. remaining detections drift away from ground-truth boxes. (localisation error,∆L); or (iv) its confidence scores stop.

reflecting detection accuracy (calibration shift,∆E). Each. mechanism has a different physical cause and demands a. different remedy. Crucially, whether a given failure mode is a. genuine property of the corruption — as opposed to an artefact. of one particular dataset’s object density, class distribution,. or annotation style — can only be established by repeating.

the analysis on an independent benchmark, and, we argue, by. measuringthat transferability rather than only describing it. qualitatively.. Prior work has not measured all four failure dimensions. simultaneously, nor validated its conclusions on more than one. dataset, nor quantifiedhow muchof a robustness taxonomy. actually transfers. Calibration under corruption, in particular,.

has received almost no attention despite its safety implications:. a model that suppresses detections is problematic, but a model. that confidently hallucinates non-existent obstacles may be. worse [15], [16].. This work. We introduceFailure Geometry— an evaluation framework. that decomposes corruption-induced degradation into the four.

dimensions above and represents each corruption-severity con-. dition as a point in the resulting four-dimensional failure space.. We further extend the framework to a second, independent. benchmark (Pascal VOC) to test whether the resulting failure. taxonomy is a property of corruptions in general or an artefact. of COCO specifically, and we go beyond qualitative replication.

by introducing quantitative instruments for measuring transfer-. ability itself. RELATEDWORK. A. Object Detection Architectures. The four models we evaluate span the main contemporary. architectural families. YOLOv8n [3] and YOLOv9c [4] belong.

to the YOLO lineage of single-stage convolutional detectors. — YOLOv9 introduces Programmable Gradient Information. (PGI) and a Generalised ELAN backbone, achieving higher. accuracy than YOLOv8 at comparable speed. DETR [6] re-. placed the conventional detection pipeline with a transformer. encoder-decoder and bipartite matching, eliminating anchor.

boxes and NMS at the cost of slower training convergence.. RT-DETR [5] retains the transformer decoder but replaces the. CNN backbone with a hybrid feature extractor, recovering. real-time speed while matching DETR-level accuracy. Two-. stage anchor-based detectors such as Faster R-CNN [7] remain. in wide deployment but are outside the scope of this study.. B. Robustness Benchmarks.

Hendrycks and Dietterich [9] established the ImageNet-C. protocol — fifteen synthetic corruption types at five severity. levels — as the standard for measuring classifier robustness.. Michaeliset al.[8] extended this to object detection, intro-. ducing COCO-C and demonstrating 30–60% mAP loss across. standard detectors. Liuet al.[10] subsequently ran the most.

comprehensive study to date: twelve representative detectors,. sixteen corruptions, two datasets (COCO-C and BDD100K-C).. Their central conclusion — that a high clean-mAP detector. can simultaneously be brittle under corruption — directly. motivates our decomposition approach. Notably, even this two-. dataset study reports onlyaggregate mAP degradationon each.

dataset; it does not ask whether a multi-dimensional failure. taxonomy computed on one dataset survives evaluation on. the other, nor does it attempt toquantifytransferability with. a predictive model or a dedicated metric. This is precisely. the question our COCO/VOC comparison, transfer-prediction. analysis, and FGTS metric are designed to answer..

Everinghamet al.[2] introduced the Pascal VOC detec-. tion benchmark, which differs from COCO in object density. (VOC images typically contain fewer, larger objects across 20. categories rather than 80), scene composition, and annotation. protocol. These differences make VOC a natural stress test for. whether a corruption-robustness taxonomy generalises or is an.

artefact of COCO’s particular statistics.. Maoet al.[11] introduced COCO-O, focusing on natural. distribution shifts (weather, sketch, cartoon) rather than syn-. thetic corruptions; Chhipaet al.[12] extended this to open-. vocabulary detectors. Neither work decomposes failure beyond. mAP, and neither cross-validates its findings on a second. detection dataset or proposes a transferability metric..

C. Calibration and Reliability. Guoet al.[14] showed that modern neural networks become. systematically overconfident under distribution shift. Pathirajaet al.[15] extended this finding specifically to object detectors,. demonstrating miscalibration in both in-domain and out-of-. domain settings. Despite this, no existing robustness bench-.

mark includes calibration as an evaluation dimension alongside. detection performance. We close this gap by including∆E. (ECE shift) as the fourth dimension of our failure vector, on. two datasets, and by showing that∆Eis itself among the. weakest-transferring dimensions across datasets.. D. Failure Analysis and Texture Bias. Geirhoset al.[18] showed that ImageNet-trained CNNs are.

systematically biased toward high-frequency texture features. rather than global shape, making them sensitive to noise. corruptions that perturb local statistics. This bias partially ex-. plains our empirical observation that YOLOv8n and YOLOv9c. show higher recall degradation than DETR under impulse. noise on COCO. Adversarial robustness work [16], [17] has.

documented hallucination-like behaviour under structured per-. turbations; we show analogous effects arise undernatural. corruptions, and that their strength is itself modulated by the. evaluation dataset — a modulation we now show is statistically. significant at the model×dataset level.. Abstract—Fairness-aware learning has moved from a nice-to-. have to a hard requirement wherever machine learning touches. consequential decisions. A growing line of work on Mixture-of-. Experts (MoE) routing takes a shortcut, though: it treats a fair. router as proof of a fair model. We show that shortcut can mis-. lead.

Routing assignments can be pushed to near-independence. from a sensitive attribute while the model’s final output keeps a. striking amount of demographic signal intact – a gap we term the. Fairness Disconnect. We propose FairRoute++, a sparse-routing. framework that regularizes latent features, routing decisions,. and predictions jointly through multi-stage adversarial training.

rather than debiasing the router alone. To make the gap measur-. able, we introduce theFairness Disconnect Index (FDI), built from. routing attenuation and residual prediction leakage. Six tabular. benchmarks – income prediction, recidivism, credit scoring,. healthcare, and a controlled synthetic setting – all show the same. behavior: driving routing mutual information toward zero barely.

dents prediction-level leakage. We then ask whether this is a. tabular quirk. It is not. Repeating the protocol on two vision. datasets (CelebA, FairFace) with a convolutional MoE, and on a. text classification benchmark, reproduces the disconnect under. a different modality and architecture. Seven classical baselines,. a prediction-level mitigation study, two independent mutual-.

information estimators, and a component ablation round out. the evidence. Across every angle we tried, one conclusion holds:. routing fairness and prediction fairness are distinct properties,. and mistaking one for the other overstates how fair a system. actually is.. Machine learning now sits upstream of decisions that used. to be made by people alone – who gets a loan, who gets. flagged as high-risk, who gets a callback. Once a model shapes. outcomes like these, demographic fairness stops being a nice-. to-have and becomes part of the specification [6], [16].

Strip away the tables, and the finding is not complicated:. routing fairness and prediction fairness are different properties,. however often the literature treats them as one. Routing mutual.

information drops sharply under regularization in every dataset. and every modality we tried; demographic information in the. final prediction, more often than not, does not follow it down.. FDI exists to catch precisely that gap, rather than settling for. either half of the picture on its own.. The mechanism is not mysterious once you look for it..

Routing is a single stop on a longer route, not the destination.. An adversary can scrub the router thoroughly while upstream. latent features – never directly targeted – keep carrying signal. that resurfaces at the prediction layer. A router with near-zero. mutual information and a leaky output are not, it turns out,. mutually exclusive..

The information-flow numbers back this reading up directly.. Attenuation clears 95% on several tabular datasets and even. higher on some vision configurations – the router really has. been cleaned. Leakage does not care. It persists regardless,. which is hard to explain unless more than one channel carries. demographic information through the network; routing is.

evidently not the only door.Nor is this specific to FairRoute++’s architecture. Plain. logistic regression, tree ensembles, ordinary neural nets – all. of them leak in a statistically detectable way even when they. clear standard fairness checks. That cross-model consistency. is a useful sanity check in its own right: FDI is picking up. something general about how fairness-aware models behave,.

not an idiosyncrasy of our particular router design.. Generalizing across modalities strengthens this reading. rather than complicating it. A convolutional MoE on face. images shows the same qualitative gap as the tabular models,. at a larger scale of leakage; a transformer-based text classifier. shows a smaller, weaker version of the same gap, exactly.

proportional to how much demographic signal the raw text. carries in the first place. That domain-sensitivity is arguably. the strongest evidence FDI is measuring something real – a. metric that inflated equally regardless of underlying signal. strength would be far less trustworthy than one that scales. with it.. The mitigation experiment is a slightly humbling coda..

A prediction-level adversary helps Equalized Odds on some. datasets but leaves FDI mostly where it was. One intervention,. at one stage, is not enough on its own – closing the disconnect. for good likely means constraining latent space, router, and. prediction head together, not picking a favorite and hoping.. For anyone building fairness-aware routing methods going.

forward, the practical upshot is straightforward: reporting. routing statistics alone is an incomplete audit. Predictions. can keep leaking well after the router looks clean, in every. modality we tested. A protocol worth trusting reports both. ends of the pipeline – what the router is doing, and what the. prediction actually reveals once it reaches a decision..

FairRoute++, in that sense, is less a finished fix than. an instrument. FDI does not replace demographic parity or. equalized odds; it sits next to them, catching a specific. and previously under-examined failure mode – routing-level. progress that quietly never reaches the prediction.. nect between routing and prediction fairness, but the study has. real edges worth naming plainly.. The tabular core still leans on structured benchmarks and. a comparatively shallow router; the vision and language ex-. tensions in Section V-K address the scale question directly,. but neither touches the multi-billion-parameter MoE models. The Fairness Disconnect identified here opens up more. directions than this paper closes.. Scaling further is the most obvious one: the vision and. language results in Section V-K establish that the disconnect.

survives a change of modality and architecture, but production-. scale MoE systems – the trillion-parameter language and. vision models this line of routing-fairness work is ultimately. aimed at – remain untested, and the disconnect could plausibly. grow or shrink at that scale.. Stronger mitigation is a second, more pressing direction.. The mitigation study here shows that suppressing routing.

IX. CONCLUSION.

The question we started with was simple: does fair routing. actually produce fair predictions? Most prior work assumesyes and moves on. Ours says: not always, and not rarely. enough to ignore.. The Fairness Disconnect Index gave us a way to put. that question on firmer footing – fold prediction leakage. and routing mutual information into one number and watch. what happens.

Across six tabular benchmarks, two vision. datasets, and a text-classification benchmark, the pattern held. with remarkably little variation: routing-level demographic. information came down reliably under FairRoute++, but a. meaningful share of it kept turning up in the final prediction. regardless. Fairness measured mid-pipeline, in short, does not.

automatically survive to the decision layer – and that holds. whether the pipeline is a shallow tabular MoE, a convolutional. vision model, or a transformer text classifier.. We did not lean on one experiment to make this case.. Information-flow analysis, significance testing, seven conven-. tional baselines, a mitigation study, two independent MI esti-.

mators, a regularizer sweep, and three separate data modalities. all point the same direction. The disconnect was not a fluke of. one estimator, one architecture, or one training run – it kept. showing up.. What we hope outlasts FairRoute++ itself is a habit: check-. ing fairness at the router and calling the job done is not. enough. Intermediate fairness and final-output fairness need.
